question: The product of three integers is \(60.\) What is the least possible positive sum of the three integers?
solution:
Negative factors are allowed. In particular,
\[
10(-1)(-6)=60,\qquad 10-1-6=3.
\]
So it remains to show that a positive sum smaller than \(3\) is impossible.

If all three integers are positive, their sum is at least \(3\). Otherwise, a positive product requires one positive integer \(p\) and two negative integers \(-a,-b\), where we may take \(1\le a\le b\). We need
\[
pab=60,\qquad p-a-b>0.
\]
The positive-sum condition implies \(a,b<p\). If \(p\le4\), then \(a,b\le3\), giving \(pab\le4\cdot3\cdot3=36\), which is too small.

Also, \(p\) must divide \(60\). The table lists every remaining possibility with \(a\le b<p\), together with its sum:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
p&(a,b)&p-a-b\\ \hline
5&(3,4)&-2\\
6&(2,5)&-1\\
10&(1,6),\ (2,3)&3,\ 5\\
12&(1,5)&6\\
15&(1,4),\ (2,2)&10,\ 11\\
20&(1,3)&16\\
30&(1,2)&27\\
60&(1,1)&58
\end{array}
\]
For each \(p\), the pairs come from \(ab=60/p\); requiring \(a\le b\) avoids repeating a pair in reverse order. Thus every possible positive sum has been covered, and the smallest is \(\boxed{3}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
